Let's go back to the park, let's have a barbecue.' Exhaustion inside, threat outside, and the people closest to them urging them to quit.

verses.text: So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows.
verses.summary: Nehemiah does two things. The first is practical: he stations the people by clans in the exposed places, armed with swords, spears and bows.
verses.deep: The pastor reads this as refusing to be lulled: 'The enemy is threatening to come in and get us, so I'm going to come up with a plan. We'll shore up the gaps and make sure we are organized by families and places, armed where protection is needed. We're going to keep our head on a swivel.' Recognizing the threat is itself part of a faithful response.

verses.text: And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes.”
verses.summary: The second thing is a speech. Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome. And fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes.
verses.deep: The pastor describes this as a goosebumps moment and reaches for a picture of a leader rallying a discouraged army. The substance is two remembrances — remember the Lord, and remember who you are doing this for. 'I know you're discouraged. I know you're tired. I know the enemy is about to kill you. And I know your friends are telling you to give up and come home. But God is faithful. God is strong. He has called you to a good work. His purposes are not pointless or fragile. He is able to sustain you.' He points to Hebrews 12:3 — consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted — and to Paul in 2 Timothy 1:12, 'I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what has been entrusted to me.' Then he tells the story of Corrie ten Boom and her sister Betsie at Ravensbrück, where Betsie urged her to thank God even for the fleas in their barracks. Corrie resisted at first; later she recorded that the infestation was what kept the guards out of their section, which is how their Bible went undiscovered and how they were able to keep reading scripture to the other women. 'Thank God for the fleas. And have somebody in your life bold enough to say to you, maybe we should just stop and remember God and remember who we're fighting for.'

verses.text: When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work.
verses.summary: God frustrates the plan, the builders learn of it, and everyone returns to the wall, each to his own work.
verses.deep: The pastor notices what the text does not say: 'It doesn't record any spectacular intervention. Sometimes God's help arrives through ordinary means.' Word simply got out that the plot was known. 'This is an ordinary way that God does an extraordinary thing.' And then the question he presses on the rest of the chapter: when the pressure relents, what do God's people do? 'Did they take a nap? Did they say, good, put your swords down?' No — they went back to work.

verses.text: From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah,
verses.summary: From that day on the workforce splits: half build, half stand armed with spears, shields, bows and coats of mail, with the leaders positioned behind the people.

verses.text: who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other.
verses.summary: Those carrying loads worked one-handed, a weapon in the other.
verses.deep: The pastor takes this as the picture of the whole chapter — dependence and responsibility held together in the same moment. They did not stop building because danger was near, and they did not pretend the danger was gone. The work continued with a weapon within reach.

verses.text: And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.
verses.summary: Every builder wore a sword at his side, and the trumpeter stayed beside Nehemiah.
verses.deep: The pastor admits he thought about bringing a trumpet into the service to make the point. The trumpeter mattered because of how spread out the work was — which is what Nehemiah explains in the next two verses.

verses.text: And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, “The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another.
verses.summary: Nehemiah names the problem the trumpet solves: the work is great and widely spread, and the workers are separated from one another along the wall.

verses.text: In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us.”
verses.summary: Wherever you hear the trumpet, rally there. Our God will fight for us.
verses.deep: The pastor draws the principle out: 'Ministry is not done in silos, nor is effective ministry done apart from being encouraged in community.' The value of gathering is seeing each other face to face — 'I thought I was the only one still working on the wall, because I didn't even see you, brother, over there. But now I see you eyeball to eyeball, and you're still working and I'm still working.' He tells of a recent men's mentoring dinner where about forty men gathered, and the common reaction afterward was 'I didn't even know this many guys were doing this. I thought it was just me.' Then he names where the trumpet sounds now: 'At 9:00 and 10:45 every Sunday morning we get a chance to gather and look each other in the eye and say, I'm glad to see you here still in the fight.' And the sentence he will not let them miss: our God will fight for us.

verses.text: So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out.
verses.summary: The work runs from the break of dawn until the stars came out, half the men holding spears the whole time.

verses.text: I also said to the people at that time, “Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day.”
verses.summary: Nehemiah tells everyone to lodge inside Jerusalem overnight — a guard by night and a labourer by day.

verses.text: So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
verses.summary: None of them took off their clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
verses.deep: The pastor uses this closing detail for the fourth response: keep working and remain watchful. 'Sometimes we get so preoccupied with the opposition that even when the opposition relents, we aren't good at getting back to the work God has called us to. We think, well, that was a tough season, I'm sure glad that's over.' Nehemiah's people did the opposite — 'we didn't even take our clothes off when we went to bed.' He points to 1 Peter 5:8: be sober-minded and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion. Pulling the chapter together: 'They've heard the insults. They felt discouragement and fear. Their strength had diminished. The work demanded more than they anticipated. Yet God sustained his people through prayer, through wise and prudent action, by renewing their remembrance of who God is, and by mutually caring for one another.' His final caution is against reading the chapter as a formula: 'I don't want to ever make a Nehemiah story a moral principle implying that you do these things and you'll be good. These things are possible when we trust the Savior, Jesus, who accomplished all of these things perfectly' — building 'not in order to be loved, but because we are loved through Jesus Christ.'

sermons.title: God Confronts Sin Within
sermons.note: Pastor Andrew Reed opens with the Dallas Cowboys of the 1990s — three Super Bowls, then a collapse that analysts trace not to losing players or being outplayed but to the owner and the head coach being unable to get along. 'That marked the beginning of a disintegration from within.' He adds Rome, which historians say disintegrated from the inside rather than being conquered from without. His observation: outside pressure often pulls people together, 'because the danger is visible and the danger is shared' — which is what chapter 4 was. 'But the more dangerous threat is often the one that develops inside.' A marriage survives financial pressure and is hollowed out by hidden bitterness; a church endures attack from outside and is weakened by gossip and selfish ambition within. The big idea: 'As God's people build together, they must address what is broken within.' He reads chapter 5 as a four-step playbook for any community — a home, a workplace, a small group, a church: recognize the hurt caused by sin, confront the sin that causes the hurt, repair the wrongs caused by the sin, and protect the community from further sin. Note that the work on the wall pauses for this: 'God is not only rebuilding a wall, he is forming a people.' He closes where the series keeps landing: 'Nehemiah is not the perfect savior when it comes to dealing with sin. There was somebody who dealt with sin in the perfect way, and that is Jesus Christ. Run to Jesus, the better Nehemiah.'

sections.1: Nehemiah Stops Oppression of the Poor

verses.text: Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers.
verses.summary: The chapter opens with a cry — but this one comes from inside the walls, and it is directed against their own Jewish brothers.
verses.deep: The pastor marks the shift from the previous chapter: 'In chapter 4, Nehemiah was listening for the sound of an enemy attacking Jerusalem. But now he hears the voice of hurting people within the community.' And he states the danger plainly: 'Sanballat and Tobiah could attack the wall, but sin could destroy the community behind the wall.' He does not let the direction of the outcry pass — 'the pain wasn't coming from strangers. It was coming from people who worshiped the same God, belonged to the same covenant community, and had stood beside them to rebuild Jerusalem and defend it. In chapter 4 they defended one another against outsiders. Now in chapter 5, some of those brothers had become the source of the danger.' He points to Psalm 55: it is not an enemy who taunts me, then I could bear it — 'but it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend.' 'It hurts when an enemy attacks you, but it feels different when someone who promised to love you betrays your trust. It hurts when the world speaks falsely about you, but it hurts differently when someone in the church spreads the story.' And the closer the relationship, he notes, the greater the capacity for both comfort and pain.

verses.text: For there were those who said, “With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive.”
verses.summary: The first of three outcries: families with many children simply need grain to stay alive.
verses.deep: The pastor sets the scene behind the complaint — a famine, likely worsened by the fact that people were on the wall rather than working their fields, possibly with enemy pressure around the city. The first group's problem is the most basic one there is: 'There wasn't enough to eat.'

verses.text: There were also those who said, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine.”
verses.summary: The second outcry: families mortgaging fields, vineyards and houses just to get grain.
verses.deep: The pastor does not let the economics stay abstract: 'Listen to the seriousness of that. We're taking loans in order just to buy groceries.' These were not luxury debts. People were putting up the land that fed them in order to eat.

verses.text: And there were those who said, “We have borrowed money for the king’s tax on our fields and our vineyards.
verses.summary: The third outcry: money borrowed to pay the king's tax on the very fields and vineyards already mortgaged.

verses.text: Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards.”
verses.summary: The complaint reaches its sharpest point. We are the same flesh as our brothers, our children are like their children — and yet our sons and daughters are being forced into slavery, with no power to prevent it.
verses.deep: The pastor hears the heart of it as a question: 'Our lives matter as much as theirs. We're Jews like they are. We worship the same God. Why are you treating us as though we don't matter?' The debts had reached the point where 'their own brothers were taking their children into slavery because they were unable to repay the debts borrowed to buy their groceries or pay taxes.' This, he says, is what sin does — 'it spreads and it hurts,' citing James 1:15, that sin when fully grown brings forth death. 'Sin frequently presents itself as private, manageable, harmless. It tells us this only affects me, no one else needs to know, I have it under control. But sin never remains as contained as it promises.' He brings it home: a father's sin trickles down to his children; a church member's gossip is not just a conversation, because 'another person's reputation is damaged and people become afraid to be honest'; a leader's pride leaves everyone around them feeling unheard. And he names the trap of judging ourselves only by intent: 'We often define sin only by what we intended, saying, I didn't mean to hurt anyone. Intent matters, but it's not the whole story.' Then the warning that gives the section its edge — visible progress can conceal serious internal decay. 'The wall was going up, but these people were being pushed down. From a distance, Jerusalem looked successful. But behind the visible progress, families were hungry, property was being lost, children were being enslaved, and brothers were exploiting brothers. A completed wall would mean very little if the people inside it destroyed one another while building it.' His prayer for his own church: 'May we never be a place that raises pretty walls while decaying on the inside.' And the correction underneath it all: 'People are not obstacles to the mission. Caring for people is part of the mission. People are the ministry.'

verses.text: I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words.
verses.summary: Nehemiah's reaction to the outcry is anger.
verses.deep: The pastor is careful to qualify it: 'Not all anger is righteous. Sometimes anger is a result of wounded pride or frustrated preferences or just a loss of control. But Nehemiah's anger was different.' It was anger that people were being harmed, that God's word was being disobeyed, and that the unity of God's people was being destroyed. 'There is a time when anger is the appropriate response to sin. We should be disturbed when people are mistreated. We should be grieved when a family is being destroyed. We should be troubled when someone uses power to exploit the weak. We should not be more concerned about keeping everything comfortable than we are about whether something is right or wrong.' He quotes a line he attributes simply to one writer: the person angry 'on the right grounds, against the right persons, in the right manner, at the right moment, and for the right length of time deserves great praise. The person who cannot feel anger at evil is a person who lacks enthusiasm for good.'

verses.text: I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, “You are exacting interest, each from his brother.” And I held a great assembly against them
verses.summary: Before he acts, Nehemiah takes counsel with himself. Then he names the sin exactly — you are exacting interest, each from his brother — and calls a great assembly.
verses.deep: The pastor loves the detail that Nehemiah talked to himself first: 'I don't feel so weird anymore.' The point is the pause. 'He considers the matter before acting. He doesn't fly off the handle. His anger produces deliberate action, not reckless reaction. Some people call uncontrolled anger courage. Other people call avoidance peace. Nehemiah does neither.' He combines moral clarity with self-control, and the pastor points to Galatians 6:1 — restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Then the naming: 'He's not saying, hey, y'all just need to be nicer.' Sin must be named before it can be addressed, and our instinct runs the other way: 'We often soften our language because we don't want to face the seriousness of our behavior. Pride becomes confidence. Gossip becomes concern and prayer requests. Greed becomes ambition. Bitterness becomes discernment. Controlling behavior becomes leadership. Cruelty becomes just being honest. But when we rename sin, we protect it.' He cites Hebrews 3:13 on the deceitfulness of sin, and warns against domesticating it: trying to tame your sin nature is like a zookeeper trying to tame a big cat — when it finally attacks, no one should be shocked, because that was always its nature. On the public assembly, he is careful to balance it against Matthew 18's pattern of starting privately: here 'a communal wrong required a communal correction,' because many families had been harmed and community leaders were the ones involved. And he notes the cost Nehemiah was willing to risk — these nobles were the people funding the project. 'If this costs us a little bit of funding for the wall, that's okay. We're going to deal with the issue.'

verses.text: and said to them, “We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!” They were silent and could not find a word to say.
verses.summary: The charge lands: we have been buying our brothers back out of slavery, and you are selling them. The accused have nothing to say.
verses.deep: The pastor draws out the contradiction: 'We delivered them from slavery, and now you're enslaving them.' They were 'rebuilding Jerusalem while repeating the very kind of oppression from which God had delivered them.' Their silence is the tell. 'There are moments when God's word exposes such a clear hypocrisy and contradiction in our lives that we have no legitimate defense. The proper response in those moments is not to develop a better argument. It is to repent.'

verses.text: So I said, “The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies?
verses.summary: Nehemiah names the real issue underneath the lending. The practice is 'not good' — and the question is whether they are walking in the fear of God, given that the surrounding nations are watching.
verses.deep: The pastor pauses on the plainness of the phrase: 'The thing that you are doing is not good. You know what that means? Bad.' But the financial practice was the visible sin; 'the fear of God was the deeper issue.' He defines it: 'living in reverence and awe before him, in the settled awareness that God is holy, God sees, God speaks with authority, and one day we will answer to him.' Had they feared God they would have obeyed what he had already commanded about the poor among them, in Exodus 22 and Leviticus 25. 'A person who fears God cannot easily reduce another person's suffering into personal opportunity. The fear of God changes how we use money, how we use power, how we use words, how we use authority — even when we could get away with doing otherwise.' Then the second half of the verse: the watching nations. 'They couldn't infiltrate the city. They couldn't attack them and they couldn't discourage them. So they just sat back and watched' — and saw God's people treating one another in a way that contradicted everything they claimed about their God. 'Sanballat and Tobiah must have been laughing. Let's just do nothing and let them destroy one another.' The application: 'Our conduct within the church affects our witness outside the church.' When believers exploit, slander or divide, the watching world concludes, 'I get that at my job and at my family dinners. Why would I come to the church and get more of it?' He is grateful for people willing to say the hard thing — Nathan telling David 'you are the man,' Paul confronting Peter when his conduct contradicted the gospel. 'A faithful friend would rather risk an uncomfortable conversation than watch sin quietly destroy us.' His questions: 'Do you have anyone you allow to tell you the truth? Can your spouse raise a concern without being punished for it? Can a pastor confront sin in your life without immediately becoming your enemy? When God exposes sin, is your first response repentance or self-defense?'

verses.text: Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest.
verses.summary: Nehemiah puts himself inside the problem: I and my brothers and my servants are lending too — let us abandon this exacting of interest.
verses.deep: The pastor notices that Nehemiah does not stand clear of it. 'I don't think Nehemiah was guilty of the same oppressive practices as the nobles. The text does not accuse him of exploiting the poor. But he recognizes that he is involved in a culture of lending money and grain, and he is willing to participate likewise in the solution.' He calls that a mark of godly leadership — not standing at a distance saying 'you people need to fix this.' Our instinct is the opposite: 'A husband says the marriage would be different if my wife would change. A wife says our home would be healthier if my husband would listen. A church member says the church would be stronger if those people would get serious.' The mature question instead is, 'Lord, is there anything I need to confess? Is there any way I contributed to this situation?' And the line he repeats for emphasis: 'Restoration requires people who are more interested in healing the community than proving that they were the least guilty person in it.'

verses.text: Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them.”
verses.summary: He tells them exactly what repentance requires: give back the fields, vineyards, olive orchards and houses, and the interest you have taken — this very day.
verses.deep: The pastor notes that Nehemiah 'doesn't settle for a vague promise that everyone will just try to do better.' He itemises it, and he dates it. And the items matter: 'The fields, the vineyards, the olive orchards weren't merely sentimental possessions. They were how families fed themselves.' Restoring the land meant restoring a family's ability to provide during a famine. 'The people didn't merely need an apology. They needed their property back.' From this he draws a three-part distinction: 'Confession acknowledges the wrong — I have sinned. Repentance turns from the wrong — I am going to stop doing this. And restitution addresses the effects of the wrong — as far as I am able, I will repair what my sin has damaged.' He names the shortcut we prefer: 'Sometimes we apologise because we want relief from our guilt, but we have little concern for the person who must continue living with the consequences. We feel better because we finally admitted what we did, while the injured person is still carrying the damage.' Godly sorrow, from 2 Corinthians 7, produces earnest action. He points to Zacchaeus, who gave half his goods to the poor and restored fourfold what he had defrauded — 'not to purchase salvation,' but as the visible fruit of having met Jesus. 'If I stole something, repentance means returning it. If I damaged someone's reputation publicly, repentance may require correcting the story with the same people who heard it.' And a guard against paralysis: 'Not every wrong can be completely repaired. But the fact that we cannot repair everything must not become an excuse for not repairing anything.'

verses.text: Then they said, “We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say.” And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.
verses.summary: They agree without argument — we will restore these and require nothing from them — and Nehemiah has the priests put them under oath.
verses.deep: The pastor admires the response: 'They don't argue about their intentions. They don't say, well, we didn't mean to. They didn't complain about Nehemiah's tone. They didn't demand sympathy for what restitution was going to cost them.' And he notes Nehemiah's realism — he 'doesn't just want to rely on the emotions of the moment,' so he binds the promise with an oath before witnesses.

verses.text: I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied.” And all the assembly said “Amen” and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.
verses.summary: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a living warning, and the assembly answers Amen. Then the line that matters most: the people did as they had promised.
verses.deep: The pastor explains the gesture — people carried possessions in the fold of a garment, so shaking it out sent everything flying. 'Nehemiah shakes it out as a visual warning. If they fail to keep their promises, may God shake you out in the same way.' It was a reminder of how serious it is to make a vow to God and not keep it. But the detail he will not let pass is the last sentence. 'The service ends, the preaching happened, everybody's like, amen, praise God. And they didn't get up and go back to their normal ways. They did as they had promised to do.' His conclusion: 'Repentance is not measured only by the sincerity of your words. It is demonstrated through the direction of your actions' — and with urgency, as in Matthew 5, where a worshipper who remembers a brother has something against him leaves the gift at the altar and goes to make it right first.

verses.text: Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor.
verses.summary: The chapter turns to Nehemiah's own record: twelve years as governor, and in all that time he never took the food allowance the office entitled him to.
verses.deep: The pastor marks the timescale: 'He's looking back over 12 years of leadership. He's not just talking about 52 days of building a wall. He is describing a sustained pattern.' And he is careful about the ethics — 'The allowance was not necessarily sinful. Government officials needed provision.' What Nehemiah understood is subtler: 'something may be within his rights and still be unwise to demand under the circumstances.'

verses.text: The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.
verses.summary: Previous governors had laid heavy burdens on the people and their servants had lorded it over them. Nehemiah did not — and he names the reason: the fear of God.
verses.deep: The pastor contrasts the two patterns: the former governors 'used their position for their own benefit. They fleeced the flock.' Nehemiah refused to continue that culture. And note where he locates the restraint — the same phrase he used to confront the nobles in verse 9. 'The fear of God — this awareness that our authority belongs to him, our conduct is seen by him, and we will answer to him. I will not establish a standard for the nobles and then not live by it myself.' The question that follows is the one that protects a community: 'The question for leadership is not, am I allowed to do this, or can anyone stop me, or do I have the right. The question is, how does my choice affect the people around me.' And: 'Christian maturity is not demonstrated by knowing our rights. It is also demonstrated by knowing when love calls us to surrender our rights.'

verses.text: I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.
verses.summary: He stayed on the wall himself, acquired no land, and put all his own servants into the work.
verses.deep: The pastor reads this as a refusal to convert a crisis into personal advantage: 'He refused to use a crisis as an opportunity for personal advancement.' Rather than acquiring property while others were losing theirs, Nehemiah and his household joined the labour.

verses.text: Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us.
verses.summary: At his own table he fed a hundred and fifty men, plus visitors from the surrounding nations.
verses.deep: The pastor does the arithmetic against his own life: 'I have six mouths to feed, and I think that's a lot. He had 150 mouths to feed. And apparently groceries were pretty high back then too.' This was not a leader eating well while others went hungry — 'I didn't sit in my dining room and say, give me steaks and potatoes and cheesecake while you guys go do the work.'

verses.text: Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.
verses.summary: The daily provision is itemised — an ox, six choice sheep, birds, and wine every ten days — and still he refused the governor's allowance, because the burden on the people was already too heavy.
verses.deep: The pastor underlines the scale: 'This wasn't symbolic generosity. This was a substantial expense.' And he states the principle the whole section has been building toward: 'Those with strength and resources and authority should not use them to increase the burdens of those already struggling.' Rules against sinful behaviour are not enough on their own — 'a healthy community needs a culture shaped by godly character.' Selflessness, he says, is what protects a community from the sin that divides it.

verses.text: Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
verses.summary: The chapter ends as a prayer: remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
verses.deep: The pastor closes by pulling the four steps back together — recognise that sin hurts, confront the sin that causes the hurt, repair the wrongs where it is in our power to repair them, and protect the community by living in humble selflessness. He restates what makes this chapter urgent: 'More devastating to a church than any attack outside the church is division and decay and sin within the church.' And he refuses to leave Nehemiah as the model: 'Nehemiah is not the perfect savior when it comes to dealing with sin. There was somebody who dealt with sin in the perfect way, and that is Jesus Christ, who died on the cross to take away our sin. To live in sin is to short-circuit the power and purity that he won on the cross.' For anyone trying to manage sin on their own: 'White-knuckle dealing with your sin isn't the answer. Running to the cross is the answer. Run to Jesus, the better Nehemiah.'
